references.text: Context for the parable: Jesus told them a parable to show that they should always pray and not give up ([ref:Luk 18:1|Luke 18:1]). The widow in verse 5 is an image of perseverance in prayer, which is the main point of the parable.

A similar parable about perseverance in prayer, where a man at midnight asks his friend for bread. Here too, the point is that the person's persistent boldness (ἀναίδεια) leads to the prayer being answered ([ref:Luk 11:5-8|Luke 11:5-8]).

Jesus applies the parable: Will not God bring about justice for his chosen ones, who cry out to him day and night? He draws a conclusion from the unjust judge to God, who is far more willing to help ([ref:Luk 18:7-8|Luke 18:7-8]).
Abraham prays persistently and boldly for Sodom, bargaining with God again and again. An early example of persistent intercession that God listens to ([ref:1 Mos 18:23-32|Genesis 18:23-32]).
God hears the cry of widows and orphans who are oppressed. The widow in Jesus' parable represents the vulnerable who cry out to God for justice ([ref:2 Mos 22:21-23|Exodus 22:21-23]).
The Lord brings justice for orphans and widows. The reluctant justice of the unjust judge is contrasted with God's character as the God of justice ([ref:5 Mos 10:17-18|Deuteronomy 10:17-18]).
God is described as a father to orphans and a defender of widows. The widow in the parable represents those whom God especially cares for ([ref:Sal 68:6|Psalm 68:6]).
Exhortation to help the oppressed, bring justice to the orphan, and defend the cause of the widow. God's care for widows is a recurring theme that underlies the parable ([ref:Jes 1:17|Isaiah 1:17]).
Paul exhorts perseverance in prayer: "Be with perseverance, stay alert in it with thanksgiving!" – the same principle of persistent prayer illustrated by the parable ([ref:Kol 4:2|Colossians 4:2]).
"Pray without ceasing" – a brief summary of the principle Jesus conveys through the parable of the persistent widow ([ref:1 Tess 5:17|1 Thessalonians 5:17]).

The martyrs under the altar cry out: "Lord, you holy and true one, how long before you judge and avenge our blood?" The word ἐκδικέω (to bring justice/avenge) is used both here and in Luke 18:5, concerning God's final righteous judgment ([ref:Åp 6:10|Revelation 6:10]).
